notes: Slot 1 = Chehabist bloc (Nahj), President Helou's governing camp. Coalition slot 2 holds Raymond Eddé's National Bloc (moved from MD slot 0, which has no popularity); in reality the Bloc is in opposition within the Tripartite Alliance with the Kataeb (slot 14) and Chamoun's NLP (slot 16). The Deuxième Bureau goes to slot 13. Pro-Syrian Ba'ath in slot 7, pro-Iraqi Ba'ath in slot 21, SSNP in slot 20 (all per MD).

0.name: Numur al-Ahrar
0.text:
The Tigers are the armed wing of Camille Chamoun's National Liberal Party. They were organized in 1968 as Christian mountain villages began arming against the rise of the Palestinian commandos. Dany Chamoun, the former president's son, commands them, and they drill openly in the Chouf and the Christian suburbs of Beirut while the state looks away.

The Tigers stand for an armed defence of Christian Lebanon, the expulsion of the fedayeen from the south and the scrapping of the Cairo Agreement. They want a strong, Western-aligned state that would call on Washington again as in 1958. Their base is Chamounist youth and clan networks, and their leverage is rifles and the Chamoun name.

1.name: Al-Nahj
1.text:
The Chehabist Bloc, known simply as al-Nahj (the Path), is the governing camp built by President Fouad Chehab after the 1958 crisis. It elected Charles Helou to succeed him in 1964 and still dominates the state through Helou, Prime Minister Rashid Karami and a web of loyal deputies, civil servants and officers. Chehab himself waits in Jounieh, ready to return in the 1970 election.

The Nahj stands for a strong, modern state above the sectarian lords: planning, roads, schools and social security for the neglected regions, cautious reforms and a careful balance between the West and Nasser's Egypt. Its leverage is patronage, the presidency and the army's intelligence service, which its enemies denounce as a police state.

2.name: Hizb al-Kutla al-Wataniyya
2.text:
The National Bloc was founded by President Émile Eddé in 1943 and is now led by his son Raymond Eddé, the Maronite deputy for Jbeil, author of the banking secrecy law. Since 1968 it has joined the Kataeb and Chamoun's National Liberals in the Tripartite Alliance against the Chehabist regime, but Eddé stays a man apart.

The Bloc stands for a secular, law-governed parliamentary state, civil liberties and the end of the army's political meddling. It opposes the armed Palestinian presence and the Cairo Agreement, and it also rejects sectarian militias. It is pro-Western and liberal in economics. Its base is Jbeil and Kesrouan and Christian professionals, and its leverage is Eddé's reputation for integrity.

3.name: Al-Hizb al-Taqaddumi al-Ishtiraki
3.text:
The Progressive Socialist Party was founded in 1949 by Kamal Jumblatt, the Druze chieftain of Mukhtara, together with intellectuals of every community. Jumblatt is minister of the interior in Rashid Karami's cabinet, and he uses the post to open political life to the left and to protect the Palestinian commandos.

The PSP wants to abolish political confessionalism, introduce land reform, progressive taxes and social security, and support the Palestinian revolution. It is non-aligned but friendly to Nasser and to Moscow. Its base combines the Druze of the Chouf and Aley with leftist students and professionals. Its leverage is Jumblatt himself, who can bring the whole Lebanese left and the Druze mountain into the street.

4.name: Al-Hizb al-Shuyu'i al-Lubnani
4.text:
The Lebanese Communist Party was founded in 1924 and has been banned since 1948, yet it works almost openly. Its 1968 congress broke with the old Syro-Lebanese leadership of Khalid Bakdash and turned to Lebanese and Arab realities. Secretary-General Nicola Shawi leads it, with younger cadres such as Georges Hawi rising quickly.

The party follows the Soviet line but is now building alliances with Jumblatt, the Nasserists and the Palestinian resistance. It demands legalization, secular democracy and social reform. Its base is Greek Orthodox and Shia workers, teachers, tobacco growers in the south and union activists in Beirut. Its leverage lies in union organization and Soviet support.

5.name: Munazzamat al-Ishtirakiyyin al-Lubnaniyyin
5.text:
The Organization of Lebanese Socialists grew out of the left wing of the Arab Nationalist Movement, which broke up after the 1967 defeat. Muhsin Ibrahim, the editor of al-Hurriya, leads it. Its members have turned from Nasserism to Marxism-Leninism and work closely with the Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine in the camps and universities.

The organization calls for revolution against the confessional system, full support for armed Palestinian struggle and an alliance of workers, peasants and students. It despises the Soviet-line communists as reformists and admires Vietnam and Cuba. Its base is radical students, young teachers and Shia migrants in Beirut's poor suburbs. Its leverage is street mobilization and close ties to the fedayeen.

6.name: Hizb al-Najjada
6.text:
The Najjadeh was founded in 1936 as a Sunni Muslim scout and youth movement, the Muslim answer to the Kataeb. It fought for independence in 1943 and sided with the Nasserist rebels in 1958. Adnan al-Hakim leads it from Beirut, where it keeps uniformed youth sections and its own newspaper.

The Najjadeh defends the Arab identity of Lebanon and the rights of its Muslims against Maronite dominance. It is hostile to Western influence, the Baghdad Pact tradition and Israel, and it supports the Palestinian commandos. Its base is the Sunni lower middle class and youth of Beirut and Sidon. Its leverage lies in disciplined cadres and its ability to rally the Muslim street.

7.name: Hizb al-Ba'th al-Arabi al-Ishtiraki – Qutr Lubnan
7.english: Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party – Lebanon Region
7.native_full: Hizb al-Ba'th al-Arabi al-Ishtiraki – Qutr Lubnan
7.text:
The Lebanese branch of the Ba'ath Party split after the 1966 coup in Damascus. The faction loyal to Salah Jadid's regime now operates as Syria's political arm in Lebanon, working through Damascus-funded cadres, the As-Sa'iqa commandos and its Beirut offices. The party is not legal, but it acts in the open.

The pro-Syrian Ba'ath preaches Arab unity, socialism and armed struggle for Palestine, and it views Lebanon as part of the Syrian Arab nation. It is anti-Western and relies on Soviet-armed Damascus. Its base is in the Bekaa, Tripoli and Akkar and among Palestinians. Its leverage comes from the Syrian border, Syrian money and Syrian intelligence.

8.name: Al-Majlis al-Islami al-Shi'i al-A'la
8.text:
The Supreme Islamic Shia Council was established by parliament in 1967 and first convened in 1969, when Imam Musa al-Sadr was elected its chairman. For the first time the Shia of Lebanon have an official body independent of the Sunni Dar al-Fatwa. Under Sadr it is rapidly becoming the voice of a long-neglected community.

The Council demands development of the south and the Bekaa, protection of the border villages from Israeli attacks, a fair share of public posts and an end to the Shia's status as second-class citizens. Sadr preaches reform and coexistence, not revolution. Its base is the Shia clergy, emigrants' money and the rural poor. Its leverage is Sadr's charisma.

9.name: Usrat al-Ta'akhi
9.text:
The Brotherhood Family Association is the network of schools, a clinic and a library that Sayyid Muhammad Husayn Fadlallah founded after he came from Najaf to the poor eastern Beirut suburb of Naba'a in 1966. Around it gathers a circle of young clerics and students linked to the Islamic Dawa movement of Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr in Iraq.

The circle preaches an activist Islam that should guide all of public life, and it rejects secular leftism, Arab nationalism and the traditional Shia notables alike. It is hostile to Israel and the West and suspicious of Moscow. Its base is displaced Shia migrants in the Beirut slums, and its leverage lies in the networks of Najaf seminarians.

10.name: Dar al-Fatwa
10.text:
Dar al-Fatwa is the official Sunni religious authority of Lebanon. Shaykh Hassan Khaled has led it as Grand Mufti of the Republic since 1966. It runs the Sunni religious courts, mosques and endowments and speaks for the community in the confessional system.

The Mufti defends Muslim rights within the National Pact, calls for a fairer share of power with the Maronites and supports the Palestinian cause, while urging moderation and order. Dar al-Fatwa is close to Saudi Arabia and the Sunni notable families of Beirut, Tripoli and Sidon. Its leverage is religious legitimacy: when the Mufti speaks, Sunni prime ministers and deputies must listen.

11.name: Hizb al-Tahrir
11.text:
Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Islamic Liberation Party, has its headquarters in Beirut, where its founder Taqi al-Din al-Nabhani lives in hiding. Lebanon's relative freedom allows the party to print its pamphlets and coordinate cells in Jordan, Syria and Iraq, although the Lebanese authorities have never licensed it.

The party rejects nationalism, democracy and every existing Arab regime as un-Islamic, and works to restore a single caliphate by winning over military officers. It considers both the American and the Soviet camps enemies of Islam. Its members are educated Sunni and Palestinian youth. Its leverage is ideological: Beirut is the nerve centre of a movement that reaches across the Arab world.

12.name: Al-Jama'a al-Islamiyya
12.text:
The Islamic Group is the Lebanese branch of the Muslim Brotherhood, formally founded in 1964 out of the Tripoli-based Ibad al-Rahman association. Its leading thinker is Fathi Yakan, a Tripoli preacher and author, and its organization is strongest in Tripoli, Beirut and Sidon.

The Group calls for Islamic education, moral renewal and a society governed by Islamic values, and it rejects both secular nationalism and communism. It supports the Palestinian cause and opposes Western influence, but it works by lawful preaching and charity, not arms. Its base is the pious Sunni middle class and students. Its leverage lies in mosques, schools and welfare networks.

13.name: Al-Maktab al-Thani
13.text:
The Deuxième Bureau is the intelligence branch of the Lebanese Army, which Fouad Chehab built into the hidden pillar of his regime. Under Colonel Gaby Lahoud it watches parties and militias, manages elections and keeps the zu'ama in line. To its enemies in the Tripartite Alliance it is the real government of Lebanon.

The Bureau's creed is order and the authority of the state: no sectarian militias, no foreign armies and no uncontrolled Palestinian bases. It works with Nasser's Cairo and the West alike. Its leverage is files, informers, money and the army's guns. Its future depends on a Chehabist victory in the presidential election due later this year.

14.name: Hizb al-Kata'ib al-Lubnaniyya
14.text:
The Kataeb, or Lebanese Phalanges, were founded in 1936 by Pierre Gemayel as a disciplined youth movement and have become the largest Christian party in Lebanon. Gemayel joined Chamoun and Eddé in the Tripartite Alliance in 1968, but the Kataeb also accept cabinet posts when the country seems in danger.

The Kataeb stand for an independent, sovereign and Christian-shaped Lebanon, the National Pact, free enterprise and family values. They oppose the armed Palestinian presence and the Cairo Agreement and keep Lebanon apart from Arab unity schemes. Their base is the Maronite middle class of Beirut and Mount Lebanon. Their leverage lies in mass membership and a growing, well-trained militia.

15.name: Jam'iyyat Masarif Lubnan
15.text:
The Association of Banks in Lebanon unites the banks that have made Beirut the financial capital of the Arab world. Gulf oil money and capital fleeing the socialist regimes of Syria, Iraq and Egypt flow into its vaults. The collapse of Intra Bank in 1966 shook the system, but the bankers and import houses remain the true masters of the economy.

The bankers defend banking secrecy, a free currency, low taxes and a weak state that leaves the economy to private hands. They want peace with the Palestinians at almost any price, as long as capital keeps flowing. Their base is a few dozen Christian and Sunni families. Their leverage is money, which every politician needs.

16.name: Hizb al-Wataniyyin al-Ahrar
16.text:
The National Liberal Party was founded in 1958 by former President Camille Chamoun after his term ended in civil war and the landing of US Marines. It is one of the strongest Christian parties, and since 1968 Chamoun has led it in the Tripartite Alliance against the Chehabist regime.

The National Liberals stand for free enterprise, open markets, low taxes and a firmly pro-Western Lebanon. They despise Nasserism, the Deuxième Bureau and the Cairo Agreement. Their base is the Christians of the Chouf, Beirut and the Metn, many Druze Yazbakis, and the business community. Their leverage is Chamoun's popularity and his ties to Washington, London and the Gulf.

17.name: Asdiqa al-Arz
17.text:
The Friends of the Cedars are foresters, mountain villagers, monks and university naturalists concerned about the last cedar groves of Bsharri, Barouk and Ehden, which are being lost to grazing goats, timber cutting and careless tourism. They also watch with alarm as unchecked construction swallows the coast and the Litani is diverted for irrigation and power.

The Friends call for protected forests, reforestation of the bare mountains, control of quarries and clean rivers. They avoid sectarian politics and speak in the name of Lebanon's national emblem. Their base is the mountain clergy, schools and village councils. Their leverage is moral: no politician wants to be seen as the man who let the cedars die.

18.name: Hay Heghapokhakan Dashnaktsutyun
18.text:
The Armenian Revolutionary Federation, the Tashnag, is the dominant party of Lebanon's Armenian community and holds the Armenian seats of Beirut and the Metn. Founded in Tiflis in 1890, it runs schools, clubs and youth movements in Bourj Hammoud. Its deputies, including Khatchik Babikian, sit in parliament.

The Tashnag is socialist in doctrine but cautious in Lebanese politics, usually siding with the established Christian leaders against Nasserism. It demands recognition of the Armenian genocide and dreams of a free, united Armenia beyond Soviet rule. Its base is the Armenian working and middle class. Its leverage is a disciplined bloc vote that every coalition seeks.

19.name: Lubnan al-Ishtiraki
19.text:
Socialist Lebanon is a small New Left group founded in 1965 by young intellectuals, among them Waddah Charara and Fawwaz Traboulsi. Its journal of the same name analyses Lebanese society through Marx, Gramsci and the Third World revolutions. It is unlicensed but tolerated, and it is gaining influence in the American University and the Lebanese University.

The group rejects both the Soviet-line communists and Arab nationalism, and looks to the Palestinian resistance, Vietnam and Mao's China for inspiration. It calls for a revolution against the confessional system and the merchant-banking elite. Its base is students and intellectuals. Its leverage is in debates rather than numbers, but it is closely tied to the fedayeen left.

20.name: Al-Hizb al-Suri al-Qawmi al-Ijtima'i
20.english: Syrian Social Nationalist Party in Lebanon
20.text:
The Syrian Social Nationalist Party was founded in Beirut in 1932 by Antun Sa'adeh. It was banned after its failed coup against President Chehab on New Year's Eve 1961, and thousands of members were imprisoned. A 1969 amnesty freed its leaders, and figures such as Abdallah Saadeh and In'am Ra'd are now rebuilding the party.

The SSNP calls for the unity of Greater Syria, a secular state and the abolition of confessionalism. Once anti-communist and pro-Western, it is now moving left and towards the Palestinian resistance. Its base is Greek Orthodox, Druze and secular youth in the Koura, the Metn and Beirut. Its leverage is ideological discipline and trained fighters.

21.name: Hizb al-Ba'th – Qutr Lubnan (al-Qiyada al-Qawmiyya)
21.native_full: Hizb al-Ba'th al-Arabi al-Ishtiraki – Qutr Lubnan
21.text:
The Lebanese Ba'athists who stayed loyal to Michel Aflaq after the 1966 split now take their orders and money from the Iraqi Ba'ath, in power in Baghdad since 1968. Their strongest figure is Abdul Majid al-Rafei, a Tripoli physician popular in the poor quarters of the northern city.

The pro-Iraqi Ba'ath preaches Arab unity under one revolutionary party, a strong nationalist state and armed struggle for Palestine, and it denounces the Damascus regime as a sectarian betrayal. Its base is in Tripoli, the Bekaa and among some Palestinians. Its leverage depends on Iraqi funding, its newspapers in Beirut and Baghdad's interest in fighting Syria on Lebanese soil.

22.name: Al-Jaysh al-Lubnani
22.text:
The Lebanese Armed Forces are a small, mainly volunteer army under a Maronite command. Their commander, General Emile Boustany, negotiated the Cairo Agreement of November 1969 with Yasser Arafat, which legalized the Palestinian commandos in the south. Chehab made the army the guardian of the state, and its officers see themselves as above the sectarian squabbles.

The officer corps wants a strong state, a disciplined army and control over the fedayeen and the militias. It is trained and equipped by the West, especially France and the United States. Its leverage is that it is the only national institution, but sectarian divisions in the ranks make any open intervention risky.

23.name: Al-Umara al-Shihabiyyun
23.text:
The House of Shihab ruled the Emirate of Mount Lebanon from 1697 until 1842, and Emir Bashir II remains a legend of Lebanese statehood. The princely family survives in Beirut, Hadath and the mountain, and the title of emir still carries prestige. Its most famous descendant today is former President Fouad Chehab.

The Shihabs stand for an old idea of Lebanon: a mountain principality where Maronites, Druze and Muslims lived under one prince, protected by France and Europe. They hold no political organization, but their name and the Chehabist regime lend the house unusual respect. Their leverage is symbolic, rooted in historical memory and the notable families of Mount Lebanon.
